subject: Re: Lumenpay SSO rollout – blocking issue on SAML mapping
snippet: Found it. Your IdP is sending the user identifier in a claim called `mail`, and our SAML handler is hardcoded to look for `email`. For the users where those happen to be the same a
body_text:
Found it. Your IdP is sending the user identifier in a claim called `mail`, and our SAML handler is hardcoded to look for `email`. For the users where those happen to be the same attribute on your side it works by coincidence; for the ~half where your directory splits `mail` from `userPrincipalName` it doesn't.

Two options: we can add `mail` as a fallback claim on our end (I can ship that Thursday), or your IT team can add an `email` claim to the assertion mapping, which is probably a five-minute change on your side. Either fixes it — happy to do ours regardless since other customers will hit the same thing eventually.

Priya

meta.action_summary: Priya will ship a fallback claim mapping by Thursday.

body_text:
Maya — good instinct to keep this tight and good instinct to be wary, though I don't think the two are in tension with taking the call. My advice, having sat through a handful of these on other boards:

Take the 30 minutes. Declining to even hear a VP of corp dev out at a company like Solvane can itself send a signal, and you learn things from the shape of the conversation even if nothing ever comes of it — how serious the mandate actually is, whether it's coming from their CEO or is Marcus freelancing, roughly what universe of outcome they're imagining. None of that costs you anything to learn.

What I'd avoid: don't share anything you wouldn't want to see in a competitor's hands, don't discuss valuation or terms in any form even hypothetically, and don't let Marcus set the pace — if he pushes for a second meeting quickly, that tells you something too, but you're under no obligation to match his tempo.

On the fundraise timing specifically: these two tracks can run in parallel without touching each other as long as you're disciplined about not letting Raj or Foundry Line hear about this from anyone but you, and not letting this conversation slow down or become a bargaining chip in the Series B process. The moment it starts functioning as leverage in either direction instead of two separate things, it gets messy.

Happy to sit in on the call if you want a second set of ears, or to debrief after if you'd rather keep the room small. Keep me posted either way — and if he mentions a number, even an informal one, tell me immediately, don't wait for our next scheduled catch-up.

A couple more things while I have the context loaded. First, worth thinking now about who inside Kettle would ever need to know, if this goes anywhere at all. My strong preference is nobody beyond the three of us plus maybe Sana for calendar logistics, until and unless there's something concrete enough to warrant a wider circle — the moment more than a handful of people know a company is fielding inbound interest, it has a way of becoming true even when it isn't, and I've seen a rumor like that spook a term sheet before, not because anything was actually wrong but because a candidate lead investor got nervous about a process they didn't fully understand.

Second, on Solvane specifically — I don't know them well, but I know two people who've dealt with their corp dev team on prior deals, one that closed and one that didn't. I'll make a couple of quiet calls this week, nothing that tips our hand, just background on how they operate and whether Marcus has real authority or is more of a scout. Should have something for you before your call with him, which will help you calibrate how much runway to give the conversation.

Third, and this is more philosophical: don't feel obligated to have a point of view yet on whether you'd actually want to sell the company. Nobody's asked you that question yet, and you don't have enough information to answer it honestly. Your only job on the first call is to gather information and protect the company's optionality — the decision about what you'd actually want, if a real number ever showed up, is a conversation for later, with more data and probably the full board in the room.

Greg

body_text:
Maya,

We're kicking off fieldwork for your Type II examination this week — good to be working with Kettle again after the readiness assessment in the spring. Wanted to send a proper overview before the item requests start landing in your inbox in bulk.

A quick refresher on scope: this is a Type II report, which means we're not just confirming that controls are designed correctly (that was the Type I work you did in Q1) but that they actually operated effectively over the full review period, which we've set as January 1 through June 30, 2026. That's the main difference people find surprising the first time through — we're not just looking at a policy document, we're sampling actual evidence across the six months to confirm the control ran the way the policy says it should.

Attached is the provided-by-client (PBC) list — ten items to start, organized by control area. I've assigned a suggested owner based on our conversations with Priya during scoping, but please reassign anything that doesn't match how your team actually splits this work; I'd rather chase the right person from the start than lose a week to a misrouted request.

A few notes on approach:

- For anything sampling-based (change management tickets, access reviews), we'll ask for the full population first and then pull our own sample rather than have you pre-select examples — auditors get twitchy about client-selected samples, for good reason.
- Evidence should be as close to the source system as possible. Screenshots are fine where there's no better export, but a CSV or PDF export beats a screenshot every time.
- We work in two-week sprints. This first batch is due by the dates on the attached list; we'll send batch two once we've worked through what comes in.

Happy to hop on a call if it's easier to walk through the list live rather than over email — just say the word. Otherwise looking forward to digging in.

One more thing worth setting expectations on now rather than in week three: because this is your first Type II cycle, we tend to see more back-and-forth on the first PBC batch than on later ones, simply because it takes a round or two to calibrate what "enough" evidence looks like for a given control. Don't read follow-up questions as a sign something's wrong — it's normal, and companies going through their second or third cycle almost never see it. We'll also be scheduling a handful of short walkthrough calls with control owners directly, mostly Dev and Priya from what I understand of your org chart, so evidence doesn't have to fully speak for itself in cases where a five-minute conversation would clear something up faster than another email round trip.

On timing for the overall engagement: assuming this first batch comes in reasonably on schedule, we're targeting substantial fieldwork completion by early August, with a draft report following two to three weeks after that. If anything about the Jan-Jun period changed meaningfully mid-year — a platform migration, a new subprocessor, a change in who has admin access to production — flag that to me directly even if it's not explicitly one of the ten items, since those are exactly the kinds of things that shape how we scope sampling.

Best,
Owen Fitch
Senior Associate, Vantage Assurance LLP

Dana,

You're right to be direct, and I'd rather you were than not. I'm sorry — both for missing June 30 and for the fact that you had to chase Dev for a straight answer instead of getting one from me.

Here's what actually happened. Your ledger schema uses a compound key structure for multi-entity transactions that our migration tooling wasn't built to handle — we discovered this three weeks into the cutover, not before, because our test dataset didn't include a multi-entity account like yours. That's on us. We should have caught it in scoping, and Priya's team is redoing our onboarding checklist so the next enterprise migration doesn't get surprised the same way.

Where we actually are: the mapping logic is rewritten and passing against a full copy of your July data in staging. What's left is a dry-run cutover rehearsal and a rollback plan we're comfortable with, given how much trust we've already spent here. I'm not going to give you a date I'm not confident in a second time, so here's the one I am confident in: July 31, with the actual cutover happening the weekend of the 25th so we have a week of headroom before I tell you it's done.

To rebuild some of that trust mechanically rather than just asking for it: you'll get a written status update from me — not Dev, not support — every Friday until this is closed out, whether or not there's news. If we slip again, I want you to hear it from me on a Friday, not discover it on your own three weeks later.

I also want to make this right on the commercial side. I'm crediting Lumenpay 100% of August platform fees regardless of how the migration lands. Wendy will get the credit memo to your AP contact this week so it's not just something I said in an email.

I can do a call today — I have 2pm and 4:30pm PT open, or tomorrow morning if today's too tight on your end. I'd rather talk than have this be the last word by email.

I know 'trust me' doesn't mean much right now. I'm hoping the Friday updates and an actual date that holds will mean more than another promise on a page, and I'd rather earn that back slowly and for real than ask you to just take my word for it a second time.

Maya

subject: Lumenpay SSO cutover — timeline
snippet: Dev — we're finalizing our Q4 enterprise launch plan on our side and the board is asking hard questions about our own vendor dependencies, Kettle included. Our security team flagge
body_text:
Dev — we're finalizing our Q4 enterprise launch plan on our side and the board is asking hard questions about our own vendor dependencies, Kettle included. Our security team flagged that our current SAML setup with Kettle is a stopgap, and we need proper SSO/SAML enforcement before we can onboard the next 200 seats — our compliance team won't sign off on expanding seat count without it.

Can you give me a real, committed date for when Kettle can ship SSO enforcement for enterprise workspaces? I know we've talked about this informally a few times since the spring — first at the QBR in April, then again when Dev mentioned it offhand on the SLA call in May — but nothing ever turned into an actual date on a calendar. I need something I can put in front of our board on the 15th of next month. If it slips again it puts our whole rollout timeline at risk, and honestly it starts to look bad for both of us given how much we've publicly talked about the Kettle partnership internally, including in our own investor updates.

For context on why this matters more than it might have a quarter ago: we signed two new enterprise logos last month who both have security questionnaires that explicitly require SSO/SAML enforcement on every vendor that touches customer data, and Kettle is on that list for both of them. Our own compliance team has started asking pointed questions about why we're still running mixed auth with a vendor at our scale. I've been running interference on this for a while, but I'm genuinely running out of runway to keep saying 'soon.'

There's also a practical piece: our provisioning workflow for new seats currently requires someone on my team to manually add each user because we can't rely on directory sync without proper SAML, which doesn't scale past a few hundred seats without someone burning a day a week on user admin. That alone is reason enough for us to want this fixed independent of the compliance angle.

Also — separately, our finance team asked if there's flexibility on the per-seat pricing once we cross 400 seats, given the direction things are trending on our side. Not urgent, just flagging it exists so it's not a surprise later.

Appreciate you, know everyone's slammed on both sides right now. Let's just get a real date on the books so I stop having to give my board a vague answer every time this comes up.

Dana

I pulled our own test suite for the SSO integration and ran it against a mirror of Lumenpay's tenant config: 40 of 42 cases pass now with the fallback claim change on our side plus their mapping fix. Will have a firmer estimate by end of week.

Priya

snippet: Raj, Appreciate you being direct — I'll try to match that. On valuation: $55-60M pre is a real conversation, but I think it undersells where we are. We closed June at $2.3M ARR, up
body_text:
Raj,

Appreciate you being direct — I'll try to match that.

On valuation: $55-60M pre is a real conversation, but I think it undersells where we are. We closed June at $2.3M ARR, up from $1.6M at the start of the year, and that's before Lumenpay's enterprise tier is even fully live — which, to be fair, is the thing giving you pause, so let me address it directly instead of talking around it.

The migration slipped because we underestimated a schema mapping problem, not because the product doesn't work at that scale — it's in staging now against their real data, cutover is the weekend of July 25, and I'm not going to pretend that slip didn't happen or that it shouldn't factor into how you're thinking about execution risk. It should, a little. But I don't think it's a $10M problem, especially with Tarrow Health scaling cleanly on the same enterprise features.

Where I'd actually push back is the framing that Series A comps from February are the ceiling — the two companies I know of that raised in that window did so before the current pullback in growth-stage multiples fully corrected, and I don't think a business at our growth rate should be priced off comps that are already stale. I'd want to talk about something closer to $70-75M pre, with the caveat that I'm more anchored to growth rate and net revenue retention than a headline number, so if there's a structure that gets you comfortable with $70M+ pre in exchange for something other than a flat valuation number, I'm open to that conversation.

On the observer seat — I don't think it's presumptuous, and honestly I'd rather have that conversation now than have it feel like a late add during diligence. My only real ask is that it's contingent on you leading, not a standing offer regardless of outcome. I think that's fair to both of us.

I'd like Ellen and Greg on the next call — partly because they'll have useful context on our board dynamics, and partly because I want you hearing the same numbers from more than just me. I'll have them loop you in with the June board numbers by end of week so you can look at the real detail before we're back on the phone.

Let's find time next week. Thursday works well on my end if it does on yours.

Maya

subject: Security addendum — Lumenpay wants SOC 2 status
snippet: Maya, Lumenpay's legal team sent over their standard security addendum as part of the enterprise expansion order — mostly boilerplate, except Section 4.2 requires us to represent t
body_text:
Maya,

Lumenpay's legal team sent over their standard security addendum as part of the enterprise expansion order — mostly boilerplate, except Section 4.2 requires us to represent that we hold a current SOC 2 Type II report, with the actual report attached as an exhibit. Their template assumes a company already has one in hand. The exact language is: 'Vendor represents and warrants that it has obtained, and shall maintain for the term of this Agreement, a SOC 2 Type II report issued within the preceding twelve (12) months, a copy of which is attached hereto as Exhibit C.' That's a representation we cannot truthfully sign today, and I don't want us in a position where we've made a written warranty that isn't accurate the day we sign it — that's the kind of thing that comes back in a dispute years later even if nobody's thinking about it now.

Given the Type II examination doesn't wrap until mid-September at the earliest, we can't make that representation truthfully today. A few options: (1) ask them to accept the SOC 2 Type I report we already have plus a bridge letter describing Type II status, (2) push the addendum's effective date to align with when the Type II report is actually ready, or (3) have Halcyon issue an interim attestation letter confirming the Type II engagement is in progress and on track, which is common enough that most enterprise security teams accept it.

For context, we did something similar with a different enterprise customer's security review back in March, before we'd even started the Type II observation period — their security team accepted a Type I report plus a written summary of our Type II engagement letter and target date, no interim attestation needed at all. Lumenpay's security team has been stricter about documentation than most of our customers so far, which is part of why I don't want to just assume they'll take the lighter-weight option without asking.

Option 3 tends to move fastest in my experience, but it's Lumenpay's security team's call whether they'll accept it in place of the full report. Want me to propose it, or would you rather loop in Dana directly first given the relationship? Either way, I'd like to get this moving this week — Section 4.2 is currently the only open item blocking the whole addendum from being executable, everything else in their template is close to final.

Priya — flagging in case there's anything about the Type II timeline I'm not accounting for.

Beth

subject: SOC 2 Type II — evidence request (access controls)
snippet: Dear Maya, As we move into the observation-period testing phase of the Type II examination (May 1 – Oct 31, 2026), we need the following evidence samples by July 31 to stay on sche
body_text:
Dear Maya,

As we move into the observation-period testing phase of the Type II examination (May 1 – Oct 31, 2026), we need the following evidence samples by July 31 to stay on schedule for our target report date of mid-September.

As a reminder of how this differs from the Type I engagement Kettle completed in February: Type I only opines on whether your controls were suitably designed as of a single point in time. Type II opines on whether those controls actually operated effectively across the full six-month observation window, which means we sample evidence throughout the period rather than taking a single snapshot at the end. This first evidence request covers the May-June portion of the window; we'll follow up with similar requests for the July-August and September-October portions as we get closer to fieldwork wrapping up.

For this round, we need:

1. Access control matrix showing role-based permissions as of a sample date in June
2. MFA enforcement logs for all admin-level accounts, June sample
3. Change management tickets for production deploys, a 25-item sample from Q2
4. Current encryption-at-rest policy documentation

On item 4 specifically: during the Type I engagement we accepted evidence of the technical control (encryption enabled) without a formal written policy document, since Type I doesn't test operating effectiveness. Type II does, and our testing standard requires a documented policy that a control actually exists and is communicated internally, not just that the technology is configured correctly. If that policy doesn't exist yet, now's the time to get it written — better to surface that gap in evidence-gathering now than have it show up as a finding in the draft report in September.

Priya, since you were our primary contact during the Type I audit, I'll direct these to you unless Maya prefers otherwise. Happy to hop on a call if anything on this list needs clarification.

One more scheduling note: our fieldwork calendar has us doing a second evidence pull covering the July-August portion of the window in early September, and a final pull covering September-October in early November, with report drafting running in parallel once each pull closes rather than waiting until the very end — that's how we're able to hold mid-September as the target for the final report despite the observation period itself running through October 31. It also means delays on early evidence, like this request, have an outsized effect on the overall timeline compared to delays later in the window, since everything downstream depends on it closing out cleanly.

Best,
Meredith Voss
Audit Senior Manager, Halcyon Assurance

Nothing is signed, nothing is close to signed, and I'd ask everyone to keep this one quiet outside this group for now — the last thing we need is speculation making its way to customers or candidates before there's anything real to say.

Wendy's got the reserved instance purchase approved, which should bring us back toward our normal run rate.

None of this is a crisis. It's just a lot moving at once, which is honestly the normal condition of a Series A company twelve months in, not a special one. I'd rather you hear the real version from me — good and complicated — than a polished one. For what it's worth, I don't think this changes the bigger picture — our internal usage numbers on the pilot group (40 users we onboarded manually back in June, before we tried to roll SSO out more broadly) are genuinely good, adoption's been high and the anomaly detection has already caught two incidents our own monitoring missed. That's exactly the story I want to be telling internally when the renewal conversation formally kicks off in Q1. I just need the SSO piece to stop being the thing that's in the way of telling it to more people.

body_text:
Your weekly SLO report for ingest-api (Jul 24 – Jul 31) is ready.

Summary
SLO target: 99.9% availability (30-day rolling)
Current attainment: 99.86%
Error budget remaining: 34% (10h 12m of the 30-day budget)
Trend: down from 61% remaining last week

What burned the budget this week
Three events accounted for nearly all of this week's burn. The largest was a 41-minute partial outage on Jul 28 (see incident #4459) caused by a connection pool exhaustion issue when the enterprise trace-view feature flag was enabled for Lumenpay's tenant, driving a 6x increase in concurrent queries against the read replica. The second was an 18-minute degradation on Jul 29 tied to the same root cause recurring after a partial rollback. The third was a smaller 6-minute blip on Jul 30 during the nightly backfill job.

Endpoint breakdown
POST /v1/traces/ingest      99.94% (target 99.9%) — healthy
GET  /v1/traces/query       98.71% (target 99.9%) — driving the miss
GET  /v1/dashboards/:id     99.98% (target 99.9%) — healthy
POST /v1/alerts/webhook     99.99% (target 99.9%) — healthy

The query endpoint is the clear outlier and matches the connection pool story above — trace-view queries hit the same replica as the standard dashboard queries and don't yet have their own connection pool or rate limit.

Recommendation
If the trace-view flag stays on for more enterprise tenants before a dedicated connection pool ships, we expect the budget to fully deplete before the 30-day window resets, which would put the team in breach of the customer-facing SLA with Lumenpay and Tarrow Health. Suggest either pausing the trace-view rollout to additional tenants or fast-tracking the connection pool work (tracked as KET-461) ahead of the currently planned Cycle 16 slot.

Historical context
This is the second week in a row the query endpoint has been the primary driver of budget burn — last week it landed at 99.90%, right at the edge of target, and the week before that it was comfortably above target at 99.97%. The trend lines up with the trace-view flag being enabled for Lumenpay on Jul 18 and then for Tarrow Health on Jul 25, which roughly doubled the number of tenants hitting the shared query path. If a third enterprise tenant is enabled before the connection pool work ships, we'd expect the query endpoint to fall below 99% for the week, which would fully exhaust the remaining 34% of budget well before the 30-day window resets on Aug 23.

Maya,

Attached is the redline on the Tarrow Health MSA renewal. Their counsel came back with two changes worth your attention before I respond: they want the liability cap raised from our standard $250K to $500K, and they added a carve-out excluding gross negligence from the cap entirely (fairly standard, not worried about that one).

The $500K ask is the real question — that's double our template and this is now your second-largest contract by ACV at $186K/year, so worth pressure-testing rather than just accepting. For reference, our only larger contract by ACV is Lumenpay, and even there we held the cap at $300K after two rounds of negotiation last year, so a jump straight to $500K for Tarrow would actually put them above our next-largest account on this specific term, which doesn't sit right to me as a starting position.

A few other differences from our template worth flagging while we're at it: they extended the renewal term from the usual 12 months to 24, which I think is fine and actually works in our favor for revenue predictability, and they added a mutual (not one-sided) confidentiality survival clause of 3 years post-termination, which is standard and not worth pushing back on.

I'd recommend countering at $350K if you want room to negotiate, or holding the line at $250K if you'd rather not open that door for future renewals — the risk with countering high is it becomes the new anchor for the next renewal in 24 months, and their counsel will remember the number. Historically Tarrow's counsel has settled within one round of whatever we counter with, based on the original MSA negotiation two years ago, so I don't expect this to drag.

Let me know how you want to play it and I'll get language back to their side by end of week.

Beth

subject: Re: Usage-based vs seat pricing – decision needed before Q4
snippet: Okay, I've been sitting with this for a few days and want to lay out where I've landed rather than just say "let's do the hybrid thing" and leave everyone guessing at the reasoning
body_text:
Okay, I've been sitting with this for a few days and want to lay out where I've landed rather than just say "let's do the hybrid thing" and leave everyone guessing at the reasoning.

Tom's right that we're leaving deals on the table, and Fenwick is the kind of logo that should be easy for us to close — 340-person eng org, exactly our ICP, and we lost it on a pricing mechanic rather than the product. That's the worst reason to lose a deal. Dev's also right that a full usage-based rebuild right now is the wrong tradeoff given where we are with Foundry Line — Raj has already asked for 12 months of revenue history in the data room, and switching to a lumpier revenue model mid-diligence would muddy that story right when we need it clean.

So: we're doing Priya's hybrid proposal. Structure is a base seat tier covering up to 15 named users with full dashboard access, plus metered API overage billed monthly above 500K calls, which per Priya's numbers should cover roughly 90% of customers within the base tier and only kick in metering for accounts that look like Fenwick. This keeps ARR from getting lumpy — the base tier is still the predictable core of revenue — while giving Tom something to close deals like this one without engineering owing us a full rebuild.

Tiers: $499/mo base (up to 15 seats), $0.02 per API call above 500K/mo, enterprise tier unchanged for anyone who wants unlimited seats and usage bundled. Luis — lock these in for the pricing page design, and let's plan to have this live before the September renewal wave starts, not just before Q4.

One more thing: I want us to grandfather existing customers on their current pricing for at least two renewal cycles rather than force a switch on them — the goal here is winning new logos we're currently losing, not re-litigating pricing with happy existing customers.

I also want to flag the thing nobody's said out loud yet: this is the second time in six weeks we've had a real disagreement play out over email across four or five people before landing somewhere, and both times it's taken the better part of a week. That's not a complaint about anyone specifically — Tom was right to push, Dev was right to slow it down, Priya's proposal is the reason we have a workable answer at all — but I think as we get closer to twelve people I want us to get faster at this, probably by putting a standing thirty-minute pricing/packaging sync on the calendar rather than relitigating things over five-person CC threads every time. I'll set that up for Thursdays starting next week.

For Tom specifically: I know this doesn't retroactively help with Fenwick, and if there's any chance of reopening that conversation once the new tiers are live, worth trying — a lot of deals that die on pricing aren't actually dead, they're just parked waiting for the vendor to fix the thing that killed them. Wouldn't blame them for having moved on, but worth one more email once we can point to a real usage-based option rather than a promise of one.

For Dev and Priya: I know hybrid billing touches the invoicing pipeline and probably Stripe's usage-based billing APIs, which I remember you flagging as somewhat immature the last time we looked at them for a different reason. If that's still true and changes the two-week estimate, tell me now rather than in week three — I'd rather move the September date than ship something rushed that generates wrong invoices for real customers.

Questions, push back now rather than after Luis starts designing.

Maya

subject: How the best Series A founders run their board meetings
snippet: Hi all, I've sat in on a lot of board meetings over the years, both as an operator and later as an advisor, and the gap between a board meeting that builds trust and one that burns
body_text:
Hi all,

I've sat in on a lot of board meetings over the years, both as an operator and later as an advisor, and the gap between a board meeting that builds trust and one that burns it usually comes down to a handful of habits. Here's what I've seen work.

1. Send the deck 48-72 hours ahead, not the night before.
This sounds obvious, but I'd guess fewer than half of Series A founders actually do it consistently. A deck that arrives the night before gets skimmed in the car on the way to the meeting. A deck that arrives three days early gets read twice, and board members show up with real questions instead of surface-level ones. The best founders I know treat the pre-read as more important than the meeting itself.

2. Lead with the bad news, not the good news.
Every founder wants to open with the win of the quarter. Don't. Open with what's off track — a slipping enterprise deal, a metric that missed plan, a hire who didn't work out — and frame it before anyone else can. Boards that hear bad news from the founder first trust the founder more, not less. Boards that discover it themselves, or hear it buried on slide 14, start wondering what else isn't being said.

3. Bring one real decision, not ten status updates.
Most board decks are 80% reporting and 20% decision-making, and it should be closer to the reverse. Pick the one or two decisions that actually need the board's input — a pricing change, a key hire, a runway-extending trade-off — and spend most of the meeting there. Status updates can live in an async pre-read.

4. Get ahead of the number that's about to change.
If a metric is about to move in a way that will surprise the board next quarter — a big customer churning, a renewal slipping, a cost line jumping — flag it this quarter, even directionally. Nothing erodes trust faster than a board member feeling blindsided by something the founder clearly saw coming.

5. End with a specific ask.
Don't let the meeting end on 'any questions?' End with 'here's what I need from each of you before we talk next' — an intro, a decision, a gut check on a hire. Boards that leave with a job to do stay engaged between meetings. Boards that leave with nothing to do drift.

If you're prepping for a board meeting in the next few weeks, I'd genuinely love to hear which of these lands hardest for you — reply and let me know.

— Lenny

snippet: Hi Maya, Open enrollment for Kettle's 2026-2027 benefits plan year opens Monday, August 10th and runs through Friday, August 21st. Here's a summary of what's changing so you can he
body_text:
Hi Maya,

Open enrollment for Kettle's 2026-2027 benefits plan year opens Monday, August 10th and runs through Friday, August 21st. Here's a summary of what's changing so you can help answer questions if employees ask.

Medical
We're moving from Anthem to Kaiser Permanente as the primary HMO option and adding a second PPO tier through Anthem for employees who want broader out-of-network coverage. Premiums for the base HMO plan are essentially flat (up about 2.1%), but the new PPO tier runs roughly 34% higher than the HMO on a per-employee basis. Company contribution stays at 85% of the HMO premium regardless of which plan an employee picks, so anyone moving to the PPO will see a bigger chunk taken from their paycheck.

Dental and vision
No changes to the dental plan (Guardian). Vision is switching carriers from VSP to EyeMed, which should be a lateral move in terms of coverage but the provider network is different, so anyone with a regular eye doctor should double check they're still in-network before the switch takes effect Oct 1.

401(k)
The employer match is increasing from 3% to 4% of salary effective the first payroll of the new plan year, which the board approved as part of the Series A comp refresh. No action needed from employees to receive the higher match — it applies automatically to anyone already contributing.

HSA/FSA
HSA contribution limits are increasing per the IRS 2027 figures ($4,300 individual / $8,550 family). FSA limits are also increasing slightly to $3,300.

What we need from you
As CEO, you don't need to do anything for your own enrollment beyond the standard elections, but Wendy may loop you in if there are questions about the PPO tier cost during the all-hands Q&A on August 12th. Happy to join that meeting if useful, especially since the option pool and comp refresh questions tend to come up in the same breath as benefits questions once people start comparing total compensation.

Timeline
Aug 10: Enrollment opens, portal live
Aug 12: All-hands Q&A session, 11am Pacific
Aug 19: Reminder email to anyone who hasn't enrolled
Aug 21: Enrollment closes at 11:59pm Pacific
Oct 1: New plan year and carrier changes take effect

One more note on timing: because the vision carrier switch (VSP to EyeMed) takes effect Oct 1 rather than at the start of enrollment, anyone with an eye appointment scheduled between now and then should double check their provider is in-network under the outgoing VSP plan, not the incoming EyeMed one — we've seen this trip people up in past years when the two dates don't line up.

Full plan comparison and rate sheets are attached to the enrollment portal at https://app.rippling.com/benefits/enrollment. If you or anyone on the team has questions before then, our support team is available at benefits-support@rippling.com or through the chat widget in the portal.

Best,
The Rippling Benefits Team

snippet: Want to make the case for reordering Q4 roadmap before we lock it for the board deck. I think enterprise RBAC and SSO hardening needs to be the top slot, ahead of the self-serve on
body_text:
Want to make the case for reordering Q4 roadmap before we lock it for the board deck. I think enterprise RBAC and SSO hardening needs to be the top slot, ahead of the self-serve onboarding revamp.

Two things pushing me here. One, the Lumenpay rollout — even after we fix the immediate SAML issue, the underlying problem is that our role-mapping was never built for customers with nested org structures, and Lumenpay won't be the last enterprise account shaped like that. Two, the SOC 2 exception Grace flagged on quarterly access reviews is exactly the kind of thing that gets worse, not better, if we don't invest in the access-control layer generally — right now a lot of our RBAC is held together by conventions the team just knows rather than anything the product actually enforces.

Self-serve onboarding is important, but nothing about it is on fire the way these two things are. I'd rather we spend Q4 making the foundation solid for the enterprise motion Tom's actually selling into, and pick self-serve back up in Q1.

Want to walk through the actual scope before you decide, because I think when people hear "RBAC and SSO hardening" they picture a small, bounded project, and it's really three separate things bundled under one label. First is the nested-group role mapping Priya's already scoping for Lumenpay — that one's small, a few days. Second is building a real permissions model with actual roles and scopes instead of the handful of boolean flags we ship today, which is closer to three weeks and touches almost every API endpoint we have. Third is SSO hardening proper — SCIM provisioning, session policies, enforced MFA for admin roles — which is another two to three weeks on top of that. Realistically this is a six-to-eight week project if we do it right instead of piecemeal, which is most of a quarter for two engineers.

I want to be honest that part of why I'm pushing this now rather than waiting for the next enterprise customer to hit the same wall is that I think we've been treating access control as a feature request instead of infrastructure, and every time we've done that historically — the original API rate limiting, the audit log system — we've paid for it later with a rushed version built under customer pressure instead of a considered one built on our own timeline. I'd rather we be the ones setting the pace on this one, especially with SOC 2 now formally on record about the access review gap. An auditor noting an exception once is a footnote. An auditor noting the same category of issue two cycles running because we never actually fixed the underlying architecture is a pattern, and patterns are what turn into real objections in an enterprise security review.

I know self-serve matters for the fundraise narrative and I'm not trying to wave that away — genuinely just think we're both right about different problems and need to pick which one bites us first if we don't fully solve either this quarter. Want to talk this through before it's locked, ideally before Friday so there's still time to adjust the deck.

meta.action_summary: Maya to decide on Q4 roadmap prioritization.

subject: Re: Roadmap: enterprise RBAC/SSO vs self-serve onboarding for Q4
snippet: I hear the argument but I disagree with the conclusion, at least on sequencing. Self-serve is how we get logos between now and whenever the Series B closes — it's the thing Raj kee
body_text:
I hear the argument but I disagree with the conclusion, at least on sequencing. Self-serve is how we get logos between now and whenever the Series B closes — it's the thing Raj keeps asking about in diligence calls, because it's the metric that tells a growth-stage investor we're not purely sales-led. If we freeze that work for a full quarter and Foundry Line asks for updated self-serve funnel numbers in October and the answer is "unchanged since July," that's a worse story to tell than "one enterprise customer had friction we're actively fixing."

I'm not dismissing the RBAC/SSO case — Lumenpay and the SOC 2 exception are real signals — I just don't think one enterprise account and one disclosed, already-remediated audit gap justify parking self-serve for three months. Feels like we're reacting to the loudest recent fire instead of the thing that actually moves the fundraise.

subject: Where things stand heading into the back half
snippet: Team, Wanted to get everyone aligned before things get busier with the board meeting and the audit converging in the next two weeks. Runway: we're sitting around 11.5 months at cur
body_text:
Team,

Wanted to get everyone aligned before things get busier with the board meeting and the audit converging in the next two weeks.

Runway: we're sitting around 11.5 months at current burn, which is fine but not generous — the Lumenpay renewal and the seat expansion Tom's been working matter more to that number than anything else on the table right now. If the 450-seat figure holds, that materially extends our runway and makes the Series B conversation a want-to, not a need-to. If it slips back down, we should assume we're raising by Q1 regardless of how the Foundry Line conversation goes.

Lumenpay: I made a commitment to Dana on the SSO date that I'm now walking back because of the SOC2 timeline collision. I take responsibility for that — we shouldn't have promised a firm date before checking it against the audit schedule, and I want us to be more disciplined about that going forward, especially with Dana given how much weight our relationship carries with their own board.

SOC2: evidence deadline moved up to the 13th per Rachel's note. Wendy and Priya, I know this is going to be a rough week, thank you in advance. If there's anything I can personally take off either of your plates to make that number, say so directly and I'll rearrange.

Hiring: the Head of Marketing search is moving — Alice sent over four strong candidates and we've got first rounds Friday. I'd like Sana and Luis in the room for at least one of those given how much of this role touches brand and product marketing together.

Board meeting: Aug 27, usual format. Sana's pulling the deck together — please get her what she's asked for on time this cycle, we were scrambling at the printer last quarter and I'd like to not repeat that.

Foundry Line: early-stage Series B conversation, nothing to announce, but Raj's team is doing real diligence, not just a warm intro call. Dev, you may hear from me about a technical diligence session with their partner soon — they'll mostly want to talk multi-tenancy architecture and SOC2 status, so it's worth having Priya on that call too.

AWS: the bill spike from June is fully explained now — it was the autoscaling group misconfiguration Priya patched last week, not organic usage growth, so there's no change to our unit economics story for the board deck. Wendy already has the credit that came back from AWS reflected in the runway model Peter sent over.

One more thing on Lumenpay specifically: the seat count on their renewal has moved around more than I'd like over the last month — 400, then 320, now apparently 450 with an EU buffer — and I don't want us building the board deck around whichever number happened to be the most recent one Tom heard on a call. Tom, can you get something in writing from Dana before it goes in the deck.

That's it for now. Appreciate everyone's work through what's been a genuinely hard stretch of overlapping deadlines — let's get through the next three weeks and then I owe the team a real breather.

Maya
